row.note: Moses writes every word spoken by YHWH before the covenant rite; this supplies a concrete Mosaic written corpus for the commentary's named sheets.
Moses reads the written covenant to the people; document and voiced instruction are joined as the commentary joins sheets with recitation.
God gives Moses two tablets written by God's finger, a material divine text rather than an anonymous past.

row.basis: Moses writes Torah and entrusts it
row.note: Moses writes Torah and gives it to the priests, a concrete transmission of Mosaic writing behind the commentary's named sheets.
Moses is told both to write a song and teach it until it is in Israel's mouths, an exact written-leaf and remembered-recited double preservation.
The song is promised not to be forgotten from descendants' mouths, closely matching S87:6's unforgotten recitation alongside durable pages.
Torah is put within people and written on their hearts, illuminating the commentary's pairing of written sheet with retained speech.
Levites read the book and give its sense so hearers understand; it concretely answers the commentary's concern that a page alone does not guarantee right reading.

row.basis: Torah scroll by scroll or whole
row.note: The debate whether Torah came in separate scrolls or as one complete book makes the commentary's distinction between individual sheets and a compiled codex a live Jewish question.
The rule distinguishing written Torah from oral transmission frames the commentary's claim that visual letters require a living vocal teaching.
Moses receives Torah at Sinai and hands it through named teachers, giving communal oral custody alongside the written Mosaic text.
The reader of Isaiah says that understanding requires a guide; this is a concrete Christian analogue to the commentary's warning that visible letters need taught interpretation.
Paul contrasts stone tablets with a message written on human hearts, a deliberate Christian reworking of external document and internal retention.
The vision is written plainly on tablets so a passerby can read it, closely matching the commentary's open, readable writing surface.
Jehoiakim cuts and burns the columns of Jeremiah's scroll, supplying a specific material danger to written leaves.
After the scroll's destruction, Jeremiah is commanded to write all the former words on another scroll; the enduring message outlives its vulnerable carrier.
God selects Abraham to command his descendants in YHWH's way of righteousness and justice, an Abrahamic teaching antecedent to content placed in ancient sheets.
The narrator says Abraham kept divine charge, commandments, statutes, and laws, a biblical basis for treating him as bearer of a divine norm before Mosaic Torah.
Rabbinic interpretation of Genesis 26:5 says Abraham fulfilled the entire Torah before Sinai, sharply expanding pre-Mosaic Abrahamic instruction.
Joshua identifies Terah's house as serving other gods, setting the inherited idolatry against which the commentary portrays Abraham's break.
This Jewish retelling has Abraham expose the helplessness of idols made by Terah and leave that world, a detailed parallel to the commentary's ancestral-idolatry scene.
Midrash's idol-smashing Abraham elaborates Genesis's terse family notice, giving an interpretive counterpart to the commentary's polemic against paternal cult.

row.basis: sun, moon, stars not to be served
row.note: Moses' warning not to serve sun, moon, or stars gives the legal-theological form of the commentary's Abraham rejecting setting luminaries.
Wisdom lists fire, wind, stars, and heavenly luminaries mistaken for gods, a close conceptual companion to the star-moon-sun scene and its Creator conclusion.

Genesis makes Abraham's sight of the stars a promise of descendants; the commentary's celestial scene instead tests and rejects a setting star as a god, so the shared nocturnal image bears a different force.
Abram builds an altar and calls on YHWH's name, giving Abraham's concrete invocation beside S87:15's remembering the Lord's name and praying.
Rabbinic tradition derives the morning prayer from Abraham, making the commentary's Abrahamic precedent for prayer explicit.
God tells Moses that the revealed name is remembered through generations, linking Moses, divine name, and enduring remembrance.
God places words in Moses and Aaron's mouths for Pharaoh, a biblical counterpart to the paired mission and spoken admonition.
Pharaoh refuses to know or obey YHWH, anchoring the commentary's portrait of the addressee who rejects Moses' warning.
Exodus has Pharaoh summon sorcerers who imitate Moses' sign; Qur'anic magicians instead reject Pharaoh, so the shared contest is a meaningful contrary telling.

row.basis: magicians name God's finger, Pharaoh hardens
row.note: The magicians acknowledge God's finger but Pharaoh remains hard; beside the commentary's converted magicians, this shows recognition without the Qur'anic confession.
God makes grass grow for cattle and plants for human use, closely matching the commentary's creator who brings out pasture and lets beasts graze.

row.basis: grass for livestock and human food
row.note: Moses' covenant instruction promises grass in the field for cattle and food for Israel, joining rain, pasture, and obedience in Mosaic teaching.
The law forbids executing child for parent or parent for child, stating that each dies for own sin; this is a direct legal analogue to the former pages' no-burden-transfer rule.

row.basis: no child or parent bears the other's sin
row.note: Ezekiel explicitly denies that child bears parent sin or parent child sin, closely restating the commentary's individual accountability.

row.basis: reward according to ways and deeds
row.note: YHWH searches heart and rewards every person according to ways and deeds, matching the pages' seen effort and full recompense.
Moses' song declares that God kills and makes alive, supplying a Mosaic formulation behind the commentary's death-life and later-resurrection contrast.
The heavenly court opens books before judgment, a precise biblical counterpart to the divine book holding what humans cannot safely retain.
Those asleep in dust awake to everlasting life or disgrace, giving the final two-outcome horizon that the commentary reads into the former sheets.
A book of remembrance is written for people who fear YHWH and esteem his name, uniquely combining divine record, fear, and name-remembrance.
The psalm locates every formed day in God's book, an analogue to Moses' assertion that former generations' knowledge is recorded with the God who does not forget.
Grass withers and fades while God's word stands forever; it tightly meets the commentary's pasture that dries and ancient written word that remains.
God promises Moses tablets of law and commandment already written, joining Mosaic writing to a prior heavenly record.
Enoch reads heavenly tablets containing human and cosmic history, expanding the commentary's unerring divine book beyond fallible page and memory.
Ezra dictates many books with five scribes, making the restoration of written revelation a focused parallel to vulnerable yet enduring pages.

row.ref: Testament of Abraham, Recension A (judgment vision; chapter numbering varies)
row.note: In the heavenly judgment vision, deeds are recorded and weighed; its Abrahamic setting makes a useful later Jewish analogue to the pages' personal effort, recompense, and final outcome.
Jesus orders treasure stored in heaven, a concrete ethical analogue to S87:16–18's refusal to prefer fleeting worldly possession to an abiding future.
Paul contrasts temporary visible things with eternal unseen realities, directly illuminating the commentary's better and more enduring final dwelling.
Citing Isaiah, the writer likens all flesh and glory to grass that withers, carrying the commentary's pasture-withering image into Christian proclamation.
The same quotation says the Lord's word remains forever, pairing durable word with v24's fading grass as the commentary does.
All appear before Christ's judgment seat to receive for personal bodily deeds, a precise Christian analogue to seen effort and recompense.
The dead are judged from opened books by their deeds, uniting individual responsibility, written record, and eschatological judgment.
Those in tombs emerge for resurrection of life or judgment according to their deeds, closely mapping the commentary's life-death and final-recompense horizon.
Each bears an individual load in Paul's responsibility argument, a concise Christian analogue to no one carrying another's moral burden.
What was written beforehand is for later instruction and hope, an explicit Christian account of why old scriptural writings still speak beside present exhortation.
Israel's earlier failures become written warnings for later readers, directly matching the commentary's old sheets as active admonition to those who turn away.
Stephen says Moses received living oracles to give the people, a Christian summary of Mosaic revelation as transmitted life-bearing speech.
Jesus' argument turns on believing Moses' writings and words; this Christian reading makes written Mosaic testimony a criterion for receiving later proclamation.

row.basis: Moses read, veil on the heart
row.note: Paul's claim that a veil lies over hearts when Moses is read is a Christian interpretive warning that reception of written text depends on the reader's heart, parallel to the commentary's page-not-self-sufficient theme.

row.basis: turn from vain things to Creator
row.note: Paul calls idol-worshipping Lystrans away from vain things to the Creator of heaven, earth, and sea, matching the commentary's Abrahamic Creator-versus-idols argument.
The Creator gives rain, fruitful seasons, and food, a Christian apostolic counterpart to the commentary's Moses creator-rain-pasture line.
Hebrews interprets Abraham's pilgrimage as seeking a city made by God, a Christian extension of the commentary's Abrahamic preference for a better, lasting future.

row.basis: Abraham's God gives life to dead
row.note: Paul identifies Abraham's God as one who gives life to the dead, recasting the commentary's Abrahamic creator-life-death confession in resurrection terms.
Christians are ransomed from futile ancestral conduct, a direct Christian idiom for the commentary's contrast between inherited idolatry and Abraham's corrective old word.

row.basis: hallowing the divine name in prayer
row.note: The model prayer begins by hallowing God's name; its named address and prayer echo the commentary's conjunction of remembering the Lord's name and praying.
The priest finds a book of Torah in the temple and sends it to be read, a counterpart to pages concealed, neglected, and again made publicly effective.
Moses prohibits adding to or subtracting from command, the Torah's own textual-ethical safeguard beside the commentary's handling and hiding of sheets.
Unlearned readers twist Paul's letters along with other Scriptures, a close Christian warning about distortion in reading written texts.

row.basis: not adding to a prophetic book
row.note: Apocalypse warns against adding to its prophetic book, extending concern for written revelation's integrity.
Isaiah's closing vision of unquenched fire supplies an older image for the commentary's great fire, though it describes corpses rather than S87's neither-dead-nor-living sufferers.
Jesus adopts Isaiah's unending-worm and unquenched-fire image, a Christian analogue to permanent punishment but not the exact neither-dies-nor-lives wording.
The everlasting covenant with Abraham and his seed makes durable words transmitted after him a biblical theme beside the commentary's lasting Abrahamic word.
Josephus credits Abraham with proclaiming one Creator rather than autonomous gods, a Jewish historical interpretation close to the commentary's creator-and-idol polemic.
God brings every hidden deed into judgment, joining the commentary's hidden and open knowledge to personal recompense and final end.
Moses carries tablets written on front and back; this adds a concrete two-faced writing surface to the commentary's material account of separately held sheets.
God says the sinner will be blotted from his book, joining Moses, a divine record, and the commentary's insistence that each person bears personal consequence.

row.basis: book placed as witness against turning away
row.note: Moses' finished Torah book is placed beside the ark as a witness against Israel; it closely parallels former sheets invoked against a person who turns away from admonition.
The king must write a copy of Torah in a book, a distinct Mosaic instance of a later custodian making and retaining a textual witness.
The written copy remains with the king for continual reading so that he may learn fear of YHWH, joining page, recitation, and fear as S87's commentary does.

row.basis: life and good, death and evil
row.note: Moses sets before Israel life with good and death with evil, a Mosaic moral choice that sharpens the commentary's two final outcomes.

row.basis: Abraham invokes God Most High and Creator
row.note: Abraham himself names YHWH God Most High, maker of heaven and earth; it tightly joins the surah's Most High title with the commentary's Abrahamic Creator confession.
Abraham prays to God and healing follows, a narrative counterpart to the commentary's Abrahamic sequence of invocation and the God who heals.

row.basis: Abraham rejects setting sun, moon, and stars
row.note: This midrash makes Abraham consider celestial lights and reject them when they set, an exceptionally close Jewish interpretive parallel to the commentary's star-moon-sun scene.
Moses asks Pharaoh how long he will refuse to humble himself before YHWH; it directly frames Pharaoh's opposite response to the purifying, fear-producing call in the commentary.
The psalmist stores God's word in the heart, a concise Hebrew counterpart to the commentary's second custody of revelation in a memorizing heart.
Wisdom draws knowledge of the Maker from the greatness and beauty of creatures, supplying the Creator-side of the commentary's Abrahamic rejection of heavenly bodies.
Rain waters earth and makes it bud and sprout, a precise scriptural companion to the commentary's divine bringing forth of vegetation and pasture.
God's word goes out and accomplishes its purpose, giving the verbal counterpart to v10's rain and supporting the commentary's enduring effective speech on old pages.
The heavens are rolled up like a scroll at cosmic judgment, an exact Hebrew image for the commentary's contrast between unrolled sheets and a rolled sky.

row.basis: sky recedes like a rolling scroll
row.note: Revelation reuses the sky-as-rolled-scroll image at the end, a Christian continuation of the commentary's eschatological page-and-cosmos imagery.

row.basis: scroll spread open, written front and back
row.note: Ezekiel's spread scroll is inscribed on front and back with lamentation and woe, a vivid textual surface that carries warning rather than merely a book's title.

row.basis: words received in heart and ears
row.note: After the scroll vision, Ezekiel is told to receive every spoken word in heart and hear it with ears; it supplies a distinct prophetic joining of internal memory and audible transmission.
Isaiah promises that the dead will live and sleepers in dust awaken, an explicit Hebrew counterpart to the commentary's other creation and final destination.

row.basis: King of the world raises to everlasting life
row.note: A martyr suffering for ancestral law expects the King of the world to raise the faithful to everlasting life, a Jewish articulation of durable afterlife tied to inherited instruction.

row.basis: Mosaic divine name read as resurrection proof
row.note: Jesus reads God's self-identification to Moses as proof that God is of the living, making a Mosaic text evidence for the resurrection taught in the former sheets.

row.basis: Scripture's message preached beforehand to Abraham
row.note: Paul says Scripture proclaimed its good news beforehand to Abraham, a Christian way of locating later saving teaching already in an Abrahamic scriptural word.
Jesus declares that heaven and earth pass away but his words do not, a sharply stated Christian counterpart to the commentary's contrast between perishing creation and enduring speech.
The world and its desire pass away while the one doing God's will remains forever, closely echoing the commentary's worldly preference versus what abides.
The final judgment separates people into eternal punishment and eternal life, a concise Christian analogue to the commentary's opposed enduring outcomes.

row.basis: scroll written inside and on back
row.note: The heavenly scroll is written within and on its back before being opened, a Christian material image that complements the commentary's pages as visible, held, and unfolded writing.
